items.label: A
items.critique: The toad joke ('We still don't know which toad') is a polished punchline; each line is a neat hook (vault trouble, renegade's tower) aimed at a quest.

items.label: B
items.critique: Flavour line, missing girl, monster with a named payer: a deliberate one-colour/one-quest/one-bounty set; 'longer than my punt' is crafted local colour.

items.label: C
items.critique: Same three-beat structure; the white-haired scout is a stock literary hook that Nox's townsfolk don't tend to deliver.

items.label: D
items.critique: Missing final period, 'strange and desperate times', a long run-on about the missing [Class] - unpolished and earnest like Nox's first village.

items.label: E
items.critique: Generic regional news (trade routes, brazen Ogres, strange noises) addressed to 'Young [Class]' - plain, unspecific Nox chatter.

items.label: F
items.critique: Disconnected one-liners incl. a bare 'Beware of the rising undead.' and an item tip about fire boots - the throwaway style of Nox's townsfolk.

items.label: G
items.critique: 'Mind your head... Ha!', a named payer for a numbered shaft, a missing cousin: the same joke/bounty/missing-person triad.

items.label: H
items.critique: Folksy 'neighborhood', 'Well good luck to ya', lowercase 'ogres' and the dumb-in-hindsight joke about building next to the ogre village - Nox's broad humour.

items.label: I
items.critique: Directions to a gossip spot and a statue, a stray remark about city breakdowns and a Chief Engineer - functional, slightly odd Nox city NPC lines.

items.label: J
items.critique: 'Last week my pig, this week my husband's boots. I'm not sure which I miss more.' and 'If he's sober, that is' are crafted punchlines; every line points at a quest.

tells: New rumour sets follow a fixed recipe: one local-colour joke, one missing-person or disaster hook, one 'X is paying gold to clear Y from Z'. Westwood's sets are looser - generic warnings, travel directions, item tips, or three variations on one complaint.
New lines end on a crafted punchline or ominous literary hook (toad, white hair, 'If he's sober'); Westwood's humour is blunter and less timed.
Westwood's townsfolk speak in general terms (trade routes, the undead, strange noises); new ones name a precise spot (ninth shaft, south pool, third plank) and a payer.
Westwood texts show small slips (missing full stop, inconsistent capitalisation of monster names, run-on sentences) and stock phrases ('strange and desperate times', 'Hail traveler').
